content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Chicken (950) is a ready‑to‑eat chicken puree specially formulated for children from 6 months old. The puree contains no added sugar, salt or preservatives and is enriched with vitamins and minerals essential for growth and development.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken meat is one of the most easily digestible protein sources for infants.
The puree is made from skinless chicken breast, reducing fat content.
It is fortified with vitamin D and iron, nutrients often lacking in toddler diets.
Texture is smooth and free of lumps to minimise choking risk.
The product meets strict European standards for infant nutrition.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken protein supports muscle growth and organ development in young children.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is essential for hemoglobin formation and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption and bone development.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using lean, skinless meat makes the puree easy on the digestive system.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Chicken provides zinc, which is important for immune function.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some children may develop an allergic reaction to chicken; introduce the product gradually.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although no salt is added, natural sodium levels may be a concern for salt‑sensitive infants.

items.title: Post‑opening storage
items.content: Once opened, keep the puree refrigerated and use within 24 hours.

items.title: Not suitable for infants under 6 months
items.content: Younger babies may have an underdeveloped digestive system for meat proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The puree is ready to serve straight from the pack. If desired, thin it with breast milk or formula to the preferred consistency. Serve warm (not hot) and always check temperature before feeding.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened packages in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated at 2‑4 °C and consume within 24 hours. Discard if the smell, colour or taste changes.

chicken-ns-as-to-part-baked-broiled-or-r.title: Chicken, skin eaten, baked, broiled or roasted

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken meat is a lean source of protein obtained from domestic poultry. It can be prepared by baking, pan‑frying, grilling or roasting. When the skin is eaten it adds flavor and a modest amount of fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is the most widely consumed meat worldwide.
It provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.
Properly cooked skin becomes crispy and aromatic.
Chicken eggs and meat are often paired in traditional dishes across cultures.
There are more than 20 chicken breeds, each with slightly different meat characteristics.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken supplies about 20–25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skin‑less chicken contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It is rich in niacin (B3), pyridoxine (B6) and cobalamin (B12), which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Chicken delivers iron, zinc and phosphorus, essential for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Selenium in chicken meat contributes to antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Bird protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in processed products
items.content: Prepared chicken items often contain added salt, which can be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Fat in the skin
items.content: Eating the skin increases saturated fat intake, potentially affecting cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken can be baked, pan‑fried, grilled or stewed. The skin can be crisped and added to salads or soups. Use the meat in salads, soups, stews, sandwiches, and Asian stir‑fries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh chicken in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. Freeze at –18 °C for up to 9 months. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any are present.

content.title: About
content.content: A chocolate sandwich consists of two soft cookies with a layer of milk or dark chocolate in between. The cookies are lightly sweetened, while the chocolate adds a creamy texture and distinctive aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate sandwich appeared in the United States in the early 1920s.
In Russia these treats are often called “chocolate wafers” or “chocolate sandwiches.”
There are many variations: milk, dark, white chocolate, and versions with nuts, caramel or sea salt.
The cookies are usually made from a soft, biscuit‑like dough.
Chocolate sandwiches are popular at children’s parties and as a coffee accompaniment.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Dark chocolate is rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates from the cookies and fats from the chocolate provides rapid energy.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Chocolate supplies magnesium, which supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Chocolate stimulates the production of serotonin and endorphins, enhancing mood.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: When made with whole‑grain flour, the cookies add dietary fiber.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Chocolate sandwiches can contain a lot of sugar, which is unsuitable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Chocolate often contains milk, which may trigger reactions in those allergic to dairy.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of cookies and chocolate makes the product energy‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: Some industrial chocolates may contain trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is convenient as a standalone snack, paired with coffee, tea, or milk. It can be cut into bite‑size pieces, added to ice cream, or used in dessert recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the chocolate sandwich in an airtight package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer storage keep it in the refrigerator to prevent the chocolate from melting.

content.title: About
content.content: Guava is a tropical fruit native to Central and South America and also cultivated in Southeast Asia. A ripe fruit has a fragrant, mildly sweet flavor with hints of strawberry and citrus, soft yellow‑green flesh, and edible seeds.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Guava is extremely rich in vitamin C: one fruit provides over 200 % of the daily requirement.
The seeds are edible and contain beneficial fatty acids.
In ancient cultures guava was used in traditional medicine to treat colds and digestive issues.
Fruits can be green or yellow depending on the variety and ripeness.
Guava is commonly used in juices, jams, desserts, and sauces.

items.title: High vitamin C content
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, helps maintain satiety, and assists in blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: These nutrients support vision, skin health, and immune function.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to guava.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet varieties have a high natural sugar level, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic fruit, it is advisable to wash or peel the skin thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Guava can be eaten fresh by cutting it in half and scooping out the flesh with a spoon. It is also suitable for juices, smoothies, salads, desserts, and sauces. The skin can be used in jams after heat treatment.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store guava at room temperature if it is not yet ripe, then move it to the refrigerator. In the fridge, a fresh fruit keeps its quality for up to 5 days. Freezing the pulp allows storage for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Pineapple (Ananas comosus) is a tropical fruit with bright yellow juicy flesh and a distinctive sweet‑tart flavor. Fresh pineapple is usually eaten raw, added to salads, desserts, juices and cocktails. It is rich in vitamins, minerals and the enzyme bromelain.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pineapple is the only cultivated member of the bromeliad family used for food.
Native to South America, it is now grown in more than 80 countries worldwide.
Bromelain, found in the core and juice, is used medically as an anti‑inflammatory agent.
Traditionally, pineapple is a symbol of hospitality and often placed at the center of festive tables.
Pineapple juice can slow blood clotting and is sometimes used as a natural anticoagulant.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One medium pineapple provides over 100 % of the daily vitamin C requirement, supporting immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains bromelain
items.content: The bromelain enzyme aids protein digestion, reduces swelling, and has anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Source of manganese
items.content: Manganese is involved in carbohydrate metabolism and protects against oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie fruit
items.content: 100 g of fresh pineapple contains about 50 kcal, making it a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy bowel function and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Bromelain allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bromelain, such as itching, swelling or hives.

items.title: High acidity
items.content: Large amounts of pineapple can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Bromelain may enhance the effect of anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), so intake should be limited when using these drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pineapple can be eaten fresh, cubed in salads, blended into smoothies, grilled, or used in desserts. For a softer texture it is sometimes lightly grilled. Pineapple juice is a popular meat marinator because bromelain tenderizes protein.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep a whole pineapple at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. Once cut, store pieces in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Freezing preserves the fruit for up to 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato French fries with chili are deep‑fried potato sticks tossed in a spicy sauce made from chili peppers, spices, and sometimes tomato base. The dish is popular in fast‑food and street‑food scenes, combining a crunchy texture with a fiery kick.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: French fries originated in Belgium in the early 19th century, while chili‑based sauces became widespread in the US during the 1970s.
Chili heat is measured on the Scoville scale; most recipes use moderately hot peppers (30‑50 000 SHU).
In Japan there is a “curry‑fries” variant where chili is blended with soy sauce and ginger.
Fries with chili are often served with cheese sauce, guacamole, or sour cream to balance the heat.
Vegan versions replace dairy dips with plant‑based mayo or cashew cheese.

items.title: Potassium source
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, an antioxidant that aids the immune system.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The tuber provides fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Capsaicin in chili
items.content: Capsaicin may boost metabolism and has mild analgesic properties.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Peptides and polyphenols from potatoes and chili help combat free radicals.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds calories; moderation is important.

items.title: Spiciness
items.content: Very hot foods can irritate the stomach of sensitive individuals.

items.title: Oil degradation
items.content: Reusing frying oil can create trans fats and harmful compounds.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some people may react to ingredients in the chili sauce.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Excess salt increases the risk of hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the fries hot, optionally sprinkling extra chili powder or fresh herbs. They are eaten by hand and can be paired with dips of your choice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or air‑fryer to restore crispness.
